claim: Plasmodium sporozoites are the mosquito-transmitted forms of the malaria parasite.
source: Plasmodium sporozoites, the mosquito-transmitted forms of the malaria parasite, first infect the liver for an initial round of replication before the emergence of pathogenic blood stages.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a definition of sporozoites.

claim: Plasmodium sporozoites first infect the liver for an initial round of replication before the emergence of pathogenic blood stages.
source: Plasmodium sporozoites, the mosquito-transmitted forms of the malaria parasite, first infect the liver for an initial round of replication before the emergence of pathogenic blood stages.
evidence: This describes the established life cycle of Plasmodium parasites.

claim: P. falciparum and P. vivax are the two main species causing malaria in humans.
source: Here we show that the two main species causing malaria in humans, Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, rely on two distinct host cell surface proteins, CD81 and the Scavenger Receptor BI (SR-BI), respectively, to infect hepatocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about malaria-causing species.

claim: P. falciparum relies on CD81 to infect hepatocytes.
source: Here we show that the two main species causing malaria in humans, Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, rely on two distinct host cell surface proteins, CD81 and the Scavenger Receptor BI (SR-BI), respectively, to infect hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing anti-CD81 antibodies inhibit P. falciparum infection.

claim: P. vivax relies on SR-BI to infect hepatocytes.
source: Here we show that the two main species causing malaria in humans, Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, rely on two distinct host cell surface proteins, CD81 and the Scavenger Receptor BI (SR-BI), respectively, to infect hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. vivax infection.

claim: CD81 and SR-BI fulfil redundant functions during infection by P. berghei.
source: By contrast, CD81 and SR-BI fulfil redundant functions during infection by the rodent parasite P. berghei.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing P. berghei can use either CD81 or SR-BI for infection.

claim: P36 is a major parasite determinant of host cell receptor usage.
source: Genetic analysis of sporozoite factors reveals the 6-cysteine domain protein P36 as a major parasite determinant of host cell receptor usage.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic complementation experiments showing P36 determines receptor usage.

claim: Malaria begins with the inoculation of sporozoites into the host skin by infected Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: Malaria begins with the inoculation of sporozoites into the host skin by infected Anopheles mosquitoes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria transmission.

claim: Sporozoites rapidly migrate to the liver and actively invade hepatocytes by forming a specialized compartment, the parasitophorous vacuole (PV).
source: Sporozoites rapidly migrate to the liver and actively invade hepatocytes by forming a specialized compartment, the parasitophorous vacuole (PV), where they differentiate into thousands of merozoites (Ménard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sporozoite behavior, supported by citation.

claim: Sporozoites differentiate into thousands of merozoites inside the parasitophorous vacuole.
source: Sporozoites rapidly migrate to the liver and actively invade hepatocytes by forming a specialized compartment, the parasitophorous vacuole (PV), where they differentiate into thousands of merozoites (Ménard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about parasite development, supported by citation.

claim: Once released in the blood, merozoites invade and multiply inside erythrocytes, causing the malaria disease.
source: Once released in the blood, merozoites invade and multiply inside erythrocytes, causing the malaria disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the malaria life cycle and pathogenesis.

claim: Infection of the liver is an essential, initial and clinically silent phase of malaria.
source: Under natural transmission conditions, infection of the liver is an essential, initial and clinically silent phase of malaria, and therefore constitutes an ideal target for prophylactic intervention strategies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the malaria life cycle.

claim: The liver stage of malaria constitutes an ideal target for prophylactic intervention strategies.
source: Under natural transmission conditions, infection of the liver is an essential, initial and clinically silent phase of malaria, and therefore constitutes an ideal target for prophylactic intervention strategies.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the essential and clinically silent nature of the liver stage.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying Plasmodium sporozoite entry into hepatocytes remain poorly understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms underlying Plasmodium sporozoite entry into hepatocytes remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Highly sulphated proteoglycans in the liver sinusoids bind the circumsporozoite protein.
source: Highly sulphated proteoglycans in the liver sinusoids are known to bind the circumsporozoite protein, which covers the parasite surface, and contribute to the homing and activation of sporozoites (Frevert et al., 1993; Coppi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The circumsporozoite protein covers the parasite surface.
source: Highly sulphated proteoglycans in the liver sinusoids are known to bind the circumsporozoite protein, which covers the parasite surface, and contribute to the homing and activation of sporozoites (Frevert et al., 1993; Coppi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sporozoite structure.

claim: Highly sulphated proteoglycans contribute to the homing and activation of sporozoites.
source: Highly sulphated proteoglycans in the liver sinusoids are known to bind the circumsporozoite protein, which covers the parasite surface, and contribute to the homing and activation of sporozoites (Frevert et al., 1993; Coppi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Subsequent molecular interactions leading to sporozoite entry into hepatocytes have not been identified yet.
source: Subsequent molecular interactions leading to sporozoite entry into hepatocytes have not been identified yet.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Several parasite proteins have been implicated in sporozoite entry, including TRAP, AMA-1, P52 and P36.
source: Several parasite proteins have been implicated, such as the thrombospondin related anonymous protein (TRAP) (Matuschewski et al., 2002), the apical membrane antigen 1 (AMA-1) (Silvie et al., 2004), or the 6-cysteine domain proteins P52 and P36 (van Dijk et al., 2005; Ishino et al., 2005; van Schaijk et al., 2008; Kaushansky et al., 2015; Labaied et al., 2007), however their role during sporozoite invasion remains unclear (Bargieri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The role of TRAP, AMA-1, P52 and P36 during sporozoite invasion remains unclear.
source: Several parasite proteins have been implicated, such as the thrombospondin related anonymous protein (TRAP) (Matuschewski et al., 2002), the apical membrane antigen 1 (AMA-1) (Silvie et al., 2004), or the 6-cysteine domain proteins P52 and P36 (van Dijk et al., 2005; Ishino et al., 2005; van Schaijk et al., 2008; Kaushansky et al., 2015; Labaied et al., 2007), however their role during sporozoite invasion remains unclear (Bargieri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD81 is one of the receptors for the hepatitis C virus (HCV).
source: Our previous work highlighted the central role of the host tetraspanin CD81, one of the receptors for the hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Pileri et al., 1998), during Plasmodium liver infection (Silvie et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CD81 is an essential host entry factor for P. falciparum and P. yoelii sporozoites.
source: CD81 is an essential host entry factor for human-infecting P. falciparum and rodent-infecting P. yoelii sporozoites (Silvie et al., 2003, 2006a).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: CD81 acts at an early step of invasion, possibly by providing signals that trigger the secretion of rhoptries.
source: CD81 acts at an early step of invasion, possibly by providing signals that trigger the secretion of rhoptries, a set of apical organelles involved in PV formation (Risco-Castillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Rhoptries are a set of apical organelles involved in PV formation.
source: CD81 acts at an early step of invasion, possibly by providing signals that trigger the secretion of rhoptries, a set of apical organelles involved in PV formation (Risco-Castillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about parasite organelles, supported by citation.

claim: CD81 binds the HCV E2 envelope protein.
source: Whereas CD81 binds the HCV E2 envelope protein (Pileri et al., 1998), there is no evidence for such a direct interaction between CD81 and Plasmodium sporozoites (Silvie et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There is no evidence for a direct interaction between CD81 and Plasmodium sporozoites.
source: Whereas CD81 binds the HCV E2 envelope protein (Pileri et al., 1998), there is no evidence for such a direct interaction between CD81 and Plasmodium sporozoites (Silvie et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence, supported by citation.

claim: CD81 acts indirectly, possibly by regulating an as yet unidentified receptor for sporozoites within cholesterol-dependent tetraspanin-enriched microdomains.
source: Rather, we proposed that CD81 acts indirectly, possibly by regulating an as yet unidentified receptor for sporozoites within cholesterol-dependent tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (Silvie et al., 2006b; Charrin et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on previous work, supported by citations.

claim: P. berghei can infect cells lacking CD81.
source: Intriguingly, the rodent malaria parasite P. berghei can infect cells lacking CD81 (Silvie et al., 2003, 2007), however the molecular basis of this alternative entry pathway was until now totally unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The molecular basis of the alternative entry pathway used by P. berghei was until now totally unknown.
source: Intriguingly, the rodent malaria parasite P. berghei can infect cells lacking CD81 (Silvie et al., 2003, 2007), however the molecular basis of this alternative entry pathway was until now totally unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: SR-BI plays a dual role during malaria liver infection, first in promoting parasite entry and subsequently its development inside hepatocytes.
source: Another hepatocyte surface protein, the scavenger receptor BI (SR-BI), was shown to play a dual role during malaria liver infection, first in promoting parasite entry and subsequently its development inside hepatocytes (Yalaoui et al., 2008a; Rodrigues et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The contribution of SR-BI during parasite entry is still unclear.
source: However, the contribution of SR-BI during parasite entry is still unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: SR-BI is also a HCV entry factor.
source: SR-BI, which is also a HCV entry factor (Scarselli et al., 2002; Bartosch et al., 2003), binds high-density lipoproteins with high affinity and mediates selective cellular uptake of cholesteryl esters (Acton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SR-BI binds high-density lipoproteins with high affinity and mediates selective cellular uptake of cholesteryl esters.
source: SR-BI, which is also a HCV entry factor (Scarselli et al., 2002; Bartosch et al., 2003), binds high-density lipoproteins with high affinity and mediates selective cellular uptake of cholesteryl esters (Acton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SR-BI function, supported by citation.

claim: Yalaoui et al. reported that SR-BI is involved indirectly during P. yoelii sporozoite invasion, by regulating the levels of membrane cholesterol and the expression of CD81 and its localization in tetraspanin-enriched microdomains.
source: Yalaoui et al. reported that SR-BI is involved indirectly during P. yoelii sporozoite invasion, by regulating the levels of membrane cholesterol and the expression of CD81 and its localization in tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (Yalaoui et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Rodrigues et al. observed a reduction of P. berghei invasion of Huh-7 cells upon SR-BI inhibition.
source: In another study, Rodrigues et al. observed a reduction of P. berghei invasion of Huh-7 cells upon SR-BI inhibition (Rodrigues et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: CD81 is not required for P. berghei sporozoite entry into Huh-7 cells.
source: Since CD81 is not required for P. berghei sporozoite entry into Huh-7 cells (Silvie et al., 2007), these results suggested a CD81-independent role for SR-BI.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The results from Rodrigues et al. suggested a CD81-independent role for SR-BI.
source: Since CD81 is not required for P. berghei sporozoite entry into Huh-7 cells (Silvie et al., 2007), these results suggested a CD81-independent role for SR-BI.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous findings.

claim: Foquet et al. showed that anti-CD81 but not anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. falciparum sporozoite infection in humanized mice engrafted with human hepatocytes.
source: More recently, Foquet et al. showed that anti-CD81 but not anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. falciparum sporozoite infection in humanized mice engrafted with human hepatocytes (Foquet et al., 2015), questioning the role of SR-BI during P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: The results from Foquet et al. questioned the role of SR-BI during P. falciparum infection.
source: More recently, Foquet et al. showed that anti-CD81 but not anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. falciparum sporozoite infection in humanized mice engrafted with human hepatocytes (Foquet et al., 2015), questioning the role of SR-BI during P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous findings.

claim: The contribution of hepatocyte surface receptors during P. vivax infection has not been investigated to date.
source: For the first time, we also explored the role of CD81 and SR-BI during hepatocyte infection by P. vivax, a widely distributed yet highly neglected cause of malaria in humans, for which the contribution of hepatocyte surface receptors has not been investigated to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: SR-BI is an important entry factor for P. vivax but not for P. falciparum or P. yoelii sporozoites.
source: Here, we show that SR-BI is an important entry factor for P. vivax but not for P. falciparum or P. yoelii sporozoites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: A monoclonal antibody against the main extracellular domain of CD81 had no effect on the number of P. vivax-infected cells in vitro.
source: A monoclonal antibody (mAb) against the main extracellular domain of CD81, previously shown to inhibit P. falciparum sporozoite infection (Silvie et al., 2003), had no effect on the number of P. vivax-infected cells in vitro (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A mouse mAb specific for SR-BI greatly reduced P. vivax infection in vitro.
source: In sharp contrast, a mouse mAb specific for SR-BI (Zahid et al., 2013) greatly reduced infection, with no additive effect of anti-CD81 antibodies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was no additive effect of anti-CD81 antibodies on the inhibition of P. vivax infection by anti-SR-BI antibodies.
source: In sharp contrast, a mouse mAb specific for SR-BI (Zahid et al., 2013) greatly reduced infection, with no additive effect of anti-CD81 antibodies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Polyclonal anti-SR-BI antibodies had the same inhibitory effect on P. vivax infection as the monoclonal antibody.
source: The same inhibitory effect was observed using polyclonal anti-SR-BI antibodies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Anti-CD81 but not anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. falciparum infection in vitro.
source: We performed the same experiments with P. falciparum sporozoites and found that anti-CD81 but not anti-SR-BI antibodies inhibit P. falciparum infection in vitro (Figure 1C), in agreement with the in vivo data from Foquet et al (Foquet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and consistent with previous in vivo data.

claim: P. vivax and P. falciparum sporozoites use distinct entry pathways to infect hepatocytes.
source: These data strongly suggest that P. vivax and P. falciparum sporozoites use distinct entry pathways to infect hepatocytes, reminiscent of the differences between P. berghei and P. yoelii (Silvie et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison with previous findings.

claim: Two distinct populations of P. vivax exo-erythrocytic forms (EEFs) could be distinguished in the infected cultures: large EEFs representing replicating schizonts, and small EEFs that may correspond to hypnozoites.
source: Two distinct populations of P. vivax exo-erythrocytic forms (EEFs) could be distinguished in the infected cultures, large EEFs representing replicating schizonts, and small EEFs that may correspond to hypnozoites (Dembele et al., 2011) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and comparison with previous findings.

claim: Anti-SR-BI antibodies reduced the numbers of large and small P. vivax EEFs to the same extent.
source: Anti-SR-BI antibodies reduced the numbers of large and small EEFs to the same extent (Figure 1E), suggesting an effect on sporozoite invasion rather than on parasite intracellular development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The effect of anti-SR-BI antibodies on P. vivax infection is on sporozoite invasion rather than on parasite intracellular development.
source: Anti-SR-BI antibodies reduced the numbers of large and small EEFs to the same extent (Figure 1E), suggesting an effect on sporozoite invasion rather than on parasite intracellular development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both large and small EEFs were equally affected.

claim: P. berghei sporozoites readily infect HepG2 cells, which lack CD81 but express high levels of SR-BI.
source: Indeed, P. berghei sporozoites readily infect HepG2 cells, which lack CD81 (Charrin et al., 2001; Berditchevski et al., 1996) but express high levels of SR-BI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), raising the possibility that this rodent parasite uses a SR-BI route to infect CD81-null cells.
evidence: This is an observation supported by previous literature and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polyclonal anti-SR-BI rabbit antibodies caused a dramatic and dose-dependent reduction of the number of P. berghei EEF-infected HepG2 cells.
source: We observed a dramatic and dose-dependent reduction of the number of EEF-infected cells induced by anti-SR-BI antibodies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Rabbit anti-SR-BI antibodies block P. berghei infection of HepG2 cells at the invasion step.
source: Quantification of host cell invasion by FACS demonstrated that the rabbit anti-SR-BI antibodies block infection at the invasion step (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar results were obtained with polyclonal rat antibodies and a mouse mAb directed against human SR-BI.
source: Similar results were obtained with polyclonal rat antibodies and a mouse mAb directed against human SR-BI (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SR-BI silencing caused a dramatic reduction of the number of P. berghei EEF-infected HepG2 cells.
source: SR-BI silencing caused a dramatic reduction of the number of EEF-infected cells (Figure 2E), but had no significant effect on the intracellular development of the few invaded parasites (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SR-BI silencing had no significant effect on the intracellular development of the few invaded P. berghei parasites.
source: SR-BI silencing caused a dramatic reduction of the number of EEF-infected cells (Figure 2E), but had no significant effect on the intracellular development of the few invaded parasites (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Plasmodium sporozoites migrate through several cells before invading a final one inside a PV.
source: Plasmodium sporozoites migrate through several cells before invading a final one inside a PV (Mota et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sporozoite behavior, supported by citation.

claim: Sporozoite cell traversal was increased in SR-BI-depleted HepG2 cells, as compared to the control.
source: Sporozoite cell traversal was increased in SR-BI-depleted HepG2 cells, as compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increase in cell traversal in SR-BI-depleted cells is likely due to the robust cell traversal activity of P. berghei sporozoites, which continue to migrate through cells when productive invasion is impaired.
source: This is likely due to the robust cell traversal activity of P. berghei sporozoites, which continue to migrate through cells when productive invasion is impaired.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: SR-BI is a major entry factor for P. berghei sporozoites in CD81-null HepG2 cells.
source: Altogether, these data establish that SR-BI is a major entry factor for P. berghei sporozoites in CD81-null HepG2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Anti-SR-BI antibodies had no inhibitory effect on P. berghei infection in HepG2/CD81 cells.
source: Strikingly, unlike in CD81-null HepG2 cells, anti-SR-BI antibodies had no inhibitory effect on P. berghei infection in HepG2/CD81 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither anti-SR-BI nor anti-CD81 antibodies alone had any significant impact on P. berghei invasion of HepG2/CD81 cells.
source: Remarkably, whilst neither anti-SR-BI nor anti-CD81 antibodies alone had any significant impact on invasion (Figure 3A) or parasite intracellular development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the combination of CD81 and SR-BI antibodies markedly reduced the number of infected cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The combination of CD81 and SR-BI antibodies markedly reduced the number of P. berghei infected HepG2/CD81 cells.
source: Remarkably, whilst neither anti-SR-BI nor anti-CD81 antibodies alone had any significant impact on invasion (Figure 3A) or parasite intracellular development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the combination of CD81 and SR-BI antibodies markedly reduced the number of infected cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Simultaneous silencing of both CD81 and SR-BI greatly reduced P. berghei infection of HepG2/CD81 cells.
source: Similarly, siRNA-mediated silencing of either CD81 or SR-BI alone had no effect on infection, whereas simultaneous silencing of both factors greatly reduced infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Blocking both CD81 and SR-BI was associated with an increase in P. berghei cell traversal activity.
source: Blocking both CD81 and SR-BI was associated with an increase in cell traversal activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the concomitant neutralization of the two host factors prevented commitment to productive invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The concomitant neutralization of CD81 and SR-BI prevented commitment to productive invasion.
source: Blocking both CD81 and SR-BI was associated with an increase in cell traversal activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the concomitant neutralization of the two host factors prevented commitment to productive invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased cell traversal.

claim: In vitro sporozoite invasion follows a two-step kinetics, with initially low invasion rates at early time points, reflecting cell traversal activity, followed by a second phase of productive invasion associated with PV formation.
source: We have shown that in vitro sporozoite invasion follows a two-step kinetics (Risco-Castillo et al., 2015), with initially low invasion rates at early time points, reflecting cell traversal activity, followed by a second phase of productive invasion associated with PV formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: In HepG2/CD81 cells, the invasion kinetics of P. berghei sporozoites in the presence of anti-SR-BI or anti-CD81 specific antibodies were comparable to those of the control without antibody.
source: In HepG2/CD81 cells, the invasion kinetics of P. berghei sporozoites in the presence of anti-SR-BI or anti-CD81 specific antibodies were comparable to those of the control without antibody (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Blocking both CD81 and SR-BI simultaneously suppressed the second phase of productive invasion of P. berghei sporozoites.
source: In sharp contrast, blocking both CD81 and SR-BI simultaneously suppressed the second phase of productive invasion (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SR-BI and CD81 are involved in the commitment to productive entry of P. berghei sporozoites.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that SR-BI and CD81 are involved in the commitment to productive entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: P. berghei sporozoites infect mouse hepatocytic Hepa1-6 cells via a CD81-dependent pathway.
source: P. berghei sporozoites infect mouse hepatocytic Hepa1-6 cells via a CD81-dependent pathway, as shown by efficient inhibition of infection by CD81 specific antibodies or siRNA (Silvie et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: SR-BI was not detected in Hepa1-6 cells.
source: Interestingly, we failed to detect SR-BI in Hepa1-6 cells (Figure 3D), providing a plausible explanation as to why CD81 is required for P. berghei infection in this model.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The absence of SR-BI in Hepa1-6 cells provides a plausible explanation as to why CD81 is required for P. berghei infection in this model.
source: Interestingly, we failed to detect SR-BI in Hepa1-6 cells (Figure 3D), providing a plausible explanation as to why CD81 is required for P. berghei infection in this model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation.

claim: Transfection of either human CD81 or human SR-BI was sufficient to rescue P. berghei infection in CD81-silenced Hepa1-6 cells.
source: Remarkably, transfection of either human CD81 or human SR-BI was sufficient to rescue infection in CD81-silenced cells (Figure 3E), demonstrating that the two receptors can independently perform the same function to support P. berghei infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CD81 and SR-BI can independently perform the same function to support P. berghei infection.
source: Remarkably, transfection of either human CD81 or human SR-BI was sufficient to rescue infection in CD81-silenced cells (Figure 3E), demonstrating that the two receptors can independently perform the same function to support P. berghei infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CD81 and SR-BI play redundant roles during productive invasion of hepatocytic cells by P. berghei sporozoites.
source: Collectively, our data provide direct evidence that CD81 and SR-BI play redundant roles during productive invasion of hepatocytic cells by P. berghei sporozoites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: P. yoelii infection was dramatically reduced by anti-CD81 antibodies.
source: P. yoelii infection was dramatically reduced by anti-CD81 antibodies, consistent with our previous work (Silvie et al., 2006a), but strikingly was not affected by anti-SR-BI antibodies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and consistent with previous work.

claim: P. yoelii infection was not affected by anti-SR-BI antibodies.
source: P. yoelii infection was dramatically reduced by anti-CD81 antibodies, consistent with our previous work (Silvie et al., 2006a), but strikingly was not affected by anti-SR-BI antibodies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: P. yoelii infection was not affected by siRNA-mediated silencing of SR-BI, but was almost abolished upon knockdown of CD81.
source: In addition, P. yoelii infection was not affected by siRNA-mediated silencing of SR-BI, but was almost abolished upon knockdown of CD81 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CD81 but not SR-BI plays a central role during P. yoelii sporozoite invasion in HepG2/CD81 cells.
source: These results indicate that CD81 but not SR-BI plays a central role during P. yoelii sporozoite invasion in HepG2/CD81 cells, similarly to P. falciparum in human hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: P52 and P36 are two micronemal proteins of unknown function previously implicated during liver infection.
source: Among potential candidate parasite factors involved in sporozoite entry, we focused on the 6-cysteine domain proteins P52 and P36, two micronemal proteins of unknown function previously implicated during liver infection (van Dijk et al., 2005; Ishino et al., 2005; van Schaijk et al., 2008; Kaushansky et al., 2015; Labaied et al., 2007; VanBuskirk et al., 2009; Mikolajczak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Genetic ablation of p52/p36 abrogates P. berghei sporozoite productive invasion of HepG2 and Hepa1-6 cells.
source: Analysis of the kinetics of PbΔp52/p36 sporozoite invasion by FACS, in comparison to control PbGFP sporozoites, revealed that genetic ablation of p52/p36 abrogates sporozoite productive invasion of HepG2 (SR-BI-dependent entry pathway) and Hepa1-6 cells (CD81-dependent entry pathway) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: PbΔp52/p36 sporozoite invasion followed similar kinetics to those observed for PbGFP sporozoites upon blockage of SR-BI or CD81, respectively.
source: PbΔp52/p36 sporozoite invasion followed similar kinetics to those observed for PbGFP sporozoites upon blockage of SR-BI or CD81, respectively, and was not modified by addition of anti-SRBI or anti-CD81 antibodies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: PbGFP but not PbΔp52/p36 parasites could form replicative PVs in both HepG2 and HepG2/CD81 cells.

claim: P52 and P36 are required for sporozoite productive invasion, in both P. berghei and P. yoelii, irrespective of the entry route.

claim: Complementation of PbΔp52/p36 with PyP52 and PyP36 restored infection in HepG2/CD81 but not in HepG2 cells.

claim: P52, although essential for sporozoite entry, is not directly associated with host receptor usage.

claim: CD81 and SR-BI define independent entry pathways for sporozoites.

evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: P. falciparum, like P. yoelii, relies on CD81 but not SR-BI.
source: We show that P. falciparum, like P. yoelii, relies on CD81 but not SR-BI, in agreement with the recent observation that antibodies against CD81 but not anti-SR-BI induce protection in humanized mice infected with P. falciparum (Foquet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and consistent with previous findings.

claim: The results are consistent with the study from Yalaoui et al. showing that in primary mouse hepatocytes antibodies against SR-BI do not inhibit P. yoelii infection when co-incubated together with sporozoites.
source: Our results are also consistent with the study from Yalaoui et al. showing that in primary mouse hepatocytes antibodies against SR-BI do not inhibit P. yoelii infection when co-incubated together with sporozoites (Yalaoui et al., 2008a).

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data that contradicts a previous model.

claim: Antibodies against SR-BI but not against CD81 inhibit infection of primary human hepatocyte cultures by P. vivax sporozoites.
source: We found that, in contrary to P. falciparum, antibodies against SR-BI but not against CD81 inhibit infection of primary human hepatocyte cultures by P. vivax sporozoites, illustrating that the two main species causing malaria in humans use distinct routes to infect hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The two main species causing malaria in humans use distinct routes to infect hepatocytes.

evidence: This is established knowledge about HCV entry, supported by citations.

evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: P. berghei can use alternatively CD81 or SR-BI to infect cells.
source: Remarkably, P. berghei can use alternatively CD81 or SR-BI to infect cells, which is surprising given that CD81 and SR-BI are structurally unrelated.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: SR-BI is structurally related to CD36.

claim: P. yoelii and P. berghei sporozoites lacking P52 and P36 reproduce the phenotype observed upon blockage of CD81 or SR-BI.
source: Here, using GFP-expressing p52 and p36 mutants and a robust FACS-based invasion assay (Risco-Castillo et al., 2015), we unequivocally establish that P. yoelii and P. berghei sporozoites lacking P52 and P36 efficiently migrate through cells but do not commit to productive invasion, reproducing the phenotype observed upon blockage of CD81 or SR-BI.
